extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in Charles Darwin's life and scientific methods (general readers, historians of science, students of scientific practice)
extracted.subtask_description: A biographical account of Charles Darwin's habits, methods, and personal qualities relevant to his scientific work and writing. The page records concrete practices, attitudes, and procedures that shaped his experimentation, note-taking, reading, and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for time / save the minutes
rubrics_metrics.description: He had a respect for time; 'saving the minutes' was the way to get work done — he noted the difference between a quarter of an hour and ten minutes' work and never wasted spare minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curtail unnecessary holidays and small delays; use short intervals productively; work up to the limit of strength and stop when necessary (example: suddenly stopping dictation with 'I believe I mustn't do any more').

rubrics_metrics.name: Never let exceptions pass unnoticed
rubrics_metrics.description: Power of never letting exceptions pass unnoticed: he seized on slight points or apparently trivial anomalies instead of accepting half-considered explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrest and examine exceptions carefully since they can be the start-point for discoveries; avoid dismissing odd facts with superficial explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doggedness / perseverance (know when to stop)
rubrics_metrics.description: He had the power of sticking to a subject and 'could not bear to be beaten' — often quoting 'It's dogged as does it'; but also felt it important to know the right point to give up an inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persist steadily in an inquiry but cultivate judgment about when to stop; recognize 'doggedness' as a virtue that can pass its right point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be an active theoriser to be a good observer
rubrics_metrics.description: He often said that 'no one could be a good observer unless he was an active theoriser.' Theorising readies the mind to see facts and magnify their importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow theory to guide observation, but remain ready to judge and discard untenable ideas; balance imaginative hypothesis-generation with critical testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to test improbable ideas ('fool's experiments')
rubrics_metrics.description: He enjoyed 'fool's experiments'—testing apparently improbable ideas (example: playing a bassoon to a plant to test sensitivity to sound vibrations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage inexpensive, playful tests of unlikely hypotheses; such trials can reveal unexpected phenomena or eliminate false leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of experiment / experiments as restorative work
rubrics_metrics.description: He enjoyed experimenting more than pure reasoning; experimental work often served as a rest or holiday from writing or abstract argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hands-on experimentation as a productive respite from analysis; use experimental work to recharge and generate fresh insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep notes of experiments, including failures
rubrics_metrics.description: He strongly urged keeping the notes of experiments which failed, and adhered to this rule himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve records of unsuccessful trials as they may contain valuable information; maintain thorough documentation to prevent loss of intellectual capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple methods and instruments first
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural tendency to use simple methods and few instruments; he preferred the simple microscope before taking to the compound and suspected work by someone who never used the simple microscope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to observe and resolve as much as possible with simple tools before resorting to more complex apparatus; simplicity can reveal fundamentals and avoid unnecessary complication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful marking and labelling of experimental materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of marking objects (e.g., tying threads of different colours, using partitions and fixed label placement so orientation became instinctive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt consistent marking conventions (colours, label placement) to prevent confusion between sample sets; make identification so habitual that labels need not be read each time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat experiments as 'sacred'—avoid wasted repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: He could not endure repeating experiments that ought to have succeeded the first time; he felt experiments were sacred and should not be wasted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments carefully to minimize the need for repetition; plan and execute with care so results are not lost to avoidable errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith in instruments but verify accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: He had faith in instrument-makers and took their accuracy for granted, yet was astonished when micrometers differed and took scrupulous pains in measurements despite rough scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust instruments but check and calibrate when possible; take careful pains with measurements even using imperfect tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical make-shift solutions acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: He often used make-shift items (darkening a box with shoe-blacking, broken glass covers) rather than elaborately made apparatus when simple solutions sufficed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer practical, low-cost solutions that meet the need; avoid over-elaboration when unnecessary, especially to conserve effort and strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe ancillary phenomena beyond the main experimental point
rubrics_metrics.description: He did not confine observation to the single point an experiment addressed but saw 'a number of other things' and thus learned as much as possible from each experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record and consider side-observations and unexpected effects; maximize the information gained from each experimental setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodical reading, marking, abstracting and cataloguing
rubrics_metrics.description: He had clear systems: unread/read book piles, pencilled marginal marks, lists of marked pages, rough abstracts under headings, and portfolios for classified facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt disciplined note-taking: mark relevant passages, compile lists, create abstracts under thematic headings, and store notes in organised portfolios for retrieval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use portfolios and organised storage for long-term facts
rubrics_metrics.description: He used portfolios (racks illustrated in his study) and large bundles of MS. marked 'used' and put away; he feared their destruction by fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise accumulated facts and manuscripts into retrievable physical (or digital) stores; protect these records from loss and damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful planning of written works (skeleton/plan and sub-headings)
rubrics_metrics.description: He spent time making a skeleton or plan of the whole work and enlarging and sub-classing each heading — primarily for presentment and arrangement of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare an overall plan and detailed sub-headings to structure argument and presentation; use planning more for clear communication than merely to develop ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose rough copy freely, then make fair copy and revise
rubrics_metrics.description: He adopted the plan of writing a rough copy straight off without attention to style, then making a fair copy (on wide-ruled paper) which was corrected and recopied before printing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate drafting and polishing: get ideas down freely in a rough draft, then edit into a fair copy and perform staged corrections before submission or publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trusted copyists/assistants for transcription and correction
rubrics_metrics.description: He relied heavily on Mr. E. Norman to copy manuscripts; he became so used to Norman's handwriting that he could not correct a manuscript until it had been recopied by him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with reliable assistants for copying and proofreading; consistent transcription can aid later revision and correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage corrections at proof/slip stage (pencil then ink)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections of slips were first written in pencil, reconsidered, then written in ink; proof correction was especially wearisome to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement corrections in draft-discernible stages to allow rethinking before finalizing; expect proof-correction to be tedious but necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be receptive to corrections and suggestions in draft stage
rubrics_metrics.description: When the book was passing through the 'slip' stage he welcomed corrections and suggestions from others (mother, sister, etc.) and was ready to be convinced an alteration was an improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit and graciously accept constructive feedback during early stages of composition; acknowledge helpful contributions and be willing to revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for obscurities and omitted logical links in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Common corrections involved fixing obscurities due to omitted necessary links in reasoning and cutting overly long sentences into clearer units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check drafts for missing connective reasoning steps and overly involved sentences; simplify sentence structure and add necessary links to preserve clarity for unfamiliar readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a courteous, conciliatory tone toward the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: His style was direct and simple; he wrote in a courteous, conciliatory tone, treating sceptical readers with patient respect and anticipating their difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address readers respectfully, expect doubt, anticipate objections, and explain points that might perplex or deter readers to facilitate understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and scrutinise illustrations; praise generously
rubrics_metrics.description: He took much interest in illustrations and perhaps over-rated them; while lavish in praise he looked closely and detected mistakes or carelessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest effort in high-quality illustrations, review them carefully for errors, and provide encouraging but precise feedback to contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horror of prolixity — keep writing concise
rubrics_metrics.description: He had a horror of being lengthy and was distressed as works grew; disliked unnecessary prolixity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for concision; prune excess material and avoid allowing works to expand beyond necessary length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and respect for other authors; strictness in attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: He spoke of other authors with respect, often apologising for rating too highly; he had a horror of laxness in quoting and a sense of literary honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sources respectfully, avoid misattribution, be scrupulous in quoting, and maintain a principled attitude toward priority and scholarly conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid engaging in priority disputes and petty reclamations
rubrics_metrics.description: He disliked questions of priority and replies to attacks ('reclamations'), viewing them as a waste of time and energy, though he sometimes departed from this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to let major issues stand on merit rather than engage in contentious priority disputes; conserve time by avoiding retaliatory public disputes where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form a critical judgement of authors' trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite respect for authors, he had a keen instinct for judging whether an author was trustworthy and used that judgement in selecting facts for argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and apply critical assessments of sources' reliability when choosing facts to cite or incorporate into an argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect and preserve manuscripts and notes against loss
rubrics_metrics.description: He felt the value of his notes strongly and had a horror of their destruction by fire; begged careful preservation in times of alarm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take concrete measures to safeguard manuscripts and notebooks (duplication, secure storage) to prevent catastrophic loss of intellectual material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical habits of measurement and care even with rough tools
rubrics_metrics.description: He used rough measuring tools (three-foot rule, apothecary's glass) but took scrupulous pains in making measurements (e.g., careful fluid-line placement, using paper scales later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with imperfect instruments, exercise meticulous technique; when possible, improve measuring tools (e.g., paper scales to millimetres) and be attentive to small procedural details.
